doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Fourth-generation New Orleanean and New Orleans food
summary: Brunious says he is a fourth-generation New Orleanean and musician, with an uncle who played with Buddy Bolden, and defends authentic Creole food.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: by anything else but what was in New Orleans, because New Orleans was pretty isolated. That’s the way I see it. You read these books and you know, people go off to the moon and different things, and you know everyone’s got a story. But that’s the way I see it. I mean I’m a fourth generation New Orleanean so I feel pretty good about saying that. Because I had an old uncle who played with Buddy Bolden, and so I’m a fourth generation musician also. And New Orleans is just a really special place in the world. I really mean that. It’s just such a great place.
And it isn’t just the people. For instance, the whole sensational palette is enlivened. The food.

Yeah, definitely. The food is the best. I can actually say that. A lot of cooks and chefs nowadays, as soon as they say something Cajun or Creole, that means add pepper to it and you can’t taste it. That is not right. That is not the way we do it there. We have spicy food, but not hot spicy. It’s spiced with like three different kinds of bell pepper, shallots, red onion, yellow onion, some pepper, quite naturally hot pepper, but not this overwhelming thing, you know, this burnt stuff they’re selling and passing off as New Orleans food. No, no, no.
